section_summary: This section begins with the conclusion of a translated plan for reorganizing Japanese industry into state-supervised economic bodies, followed by diplomatic, military, naval, consular, and FBI reporting on Japan’s deteriorating wartime economy. The reports describe rationing, shortages of labor, fuel, metals, food, and consumer goods; expanded powers under the National General Mobilization Law; censorship of economic information; transport and shipping problems; and contemporary assessments of Japanese policy and morale. The section concludes with British questions about Japan’s ability to sustain war under blockade and the opening chapters of a detailed U.S. economic estimate of Japan’s resources, trade dependence, agriculture, fishing, food supply, and livestock.

subfiles.title: Industrial Structure and Economic Bodies (continuation)
subfiles.about: Continuation of a Japanese plan for reorganizing private industry and economic associations under state guidance.
subfiles.summary: The plan retains private management as the general rule but permits restrictions, mergers, profit controls, compulsory reserves, and state guidance intended to maximize national production. It also defines government-supervised economic bodies that would help formulate and execute policy, inspect production, support sacrificed industries, and coordinate with the Imperial Rule Assistance Association.

subfiles.title: Routing memorandum on Tokyo despatch no. 5437
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Recommends reading the full account of Ambassador Grew’s conversation with Australian Minister Sir John Latham.
subfiles.summary: The note identifies Tokyo despatch no. 5437 of March 12, 1941, concerning Japanese economic conditions. It calls particular attention to the complete record of Grew’s conversation with Latham.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 5437: Transmitting Memorandum of Conversation Concerning Economic Conditions in Japan
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards a memorandum of Grew’s March 6 conversation with Sir John Latham about Japan’s economy and Australian-Japanese relations.
subfiles.summary: Grew links the enclosure to an earlier confidential telegram reporting deterioration in Japanese economic conditions. He states that Latham supplied concrete examples obtained from Japanese businessmen and also discussed broader relations between Japan and Australia.

subfiles.title: Conversation: The American Ambassador, Mr. Grew, with the Australian Minister, Sir John G. Latham
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew
subfiles.about: Records Latham’s observations on Japanese shortages, wool negotiations, immigration arguments, and public-opinion polling.
subfiles.summary: Latham describes severe bottlenecks involving housing materials, cement, pencil components, glassmaking inputs, transport, and labor. He recounts resisting Vice Foreign Minister Ōhashi’s pressure for Australian wool and compares Australian immigration restrictions with Japan’s exclusion of cheaper Chinese and Korean labor. The conversation ends with a disagreement between Latham and Grew over the value of Gallup and other public-opinion polls.

subfiles.title: Letter transmitting notes from the Nippon Yusen Kaisha Year Book
subfiles.from: J. Edgar Hoover, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Transmits extracts on Japanese labor shortages, rationing, substitute motor fuels, and synthetic-fuel production.
subfiles.summary: The cited yearbook describes shortages of skilled labor, controls on employment, prohibitions on luxury production, and rationing of sugar and matches in major cities. Additional notes discuss the replacement of charcoal-gas vehicles by acetylene-powered cars and the development of synthetic fuel at the Ōmuta and Kawasaki plants. Copies were sent to naval and military intelligence leaders.

subfiles.title: Summary of M.I.D. report no. 10,343 on the National Mobilization Law
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck / Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Summarizes a Military Intelligence Division report on Japan’s strengthened National Mobilization Law.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum emphasizes that the revision gives the Japanese Government sweeping authority over business investment, equipment, prices, combinations, and individual activity. It characterizes the law as nearly the maximum possible effort to direct the country during the emergency and notes that a translation is enclosed.

subfiles.title: Military Attaché Report no. 10,343: Revision of National Mobilization Law
subfiles.from: Harry I. T. Creswell, Military Attaché, Tokyo
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Division, War Department General Staff
subfiles.about: Analyzes article-by-article revisions expanding Japanese governmental control over economic and financial activity.
subfiles.summary: The report explains that the Diet rapidly adopted extensive revisions after weaknesses and loopholes appeared in the 1938 law. It discusses expanded control over labor, goods, finance, land, patents, industrial equipment, enterprise organization, prices, compensation, and penalties. Creswell concludes that the revised statute gives the government almost complete control over the national economy and many activities of individuals.

subfiles.title: Translation of the revised National General Mobilization Law
subfiles.from: Japanese Government, translated for the Military Attaché report
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Division, War Department General Staff
subfiles.about: Provides the translated text of the revised Japanese mobilization statute and its enforcement provisions.
subfiles.summary: The statute defines mobilization goods and businesses and authorizes conscription of labor, control or expropriation of property, regulation of finance and prices, compulsory industrial organizations, and direction of research and training. Its later articles establish compensation mechanisms, inspection powers, criminal penalties, bribery offenses, and national mobilization commissions.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of report no. 12 on economic conditions in Japan
subfiles.from: R. L. Maxwell, Administrator of Export Control
subfiles.to: Chief, Division of Controls, Department of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of a commercial attaché’s report on Japanese economic conditions.
subfiles.summary: Maxwell confirms receipt of the State Department’s December 4 memorandum enclosing report no. 12 from the commercial attaché in Tokyo. Pages 238 and 239 contain substantially identical copies of the acknowledgment.

subfiles.title: Cessation of Publication of Mitsubishi Economic Research Bureau’s Monthly Circular
subfiles.from: Samuel Sokobin, American Consulate, Kobe
subfiles.about: Reports suspension of a major Japanese economic-statistics periodical under the National Defence Security Law.
subfiles.summary: The Mitsubishi Economic Research Bureau ended its Monthly Circular with the April 1941 issue because the new security law imposed grave restrictions on economic reporting. Sokobin observes that, despite doubts about the reliability of Japanese statistics, the journal had been valuable to students assessing Japan’s economic strength and would be especially missed amid international debate.

subfiles.title: Navy memorandum transmitting A. T. HeMyer’s report
subfiles.from: H. E. Keisker, Office of Naval Intelligence
subfiles.about: Transmits a Twelfth Naval District report based on information supplied by A. T. HeMyer after his arrival from Japan.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum states that HeMyer arrived in San Francisco aboard the Tatsuta Maru on July 30, 1941. The referenced report concerns current conditions in Japan, but its text is not reproduced on this page.

subfiles.title: Navy memorandum transmitting a Twelfth Naval District report
subfiles.from: H. F. Kingman, Office of Naval Intelligence
subfiles.about: Forwards a naval report on economic conditions in Japan to the State Department.
subfiles.summary: Kingman states that the attached report came from the Commandant of the Twelfth Naval District. He sends it to Orme Wilson as information potentially useful to the State Department.

subfiles.title: Investigation Report: Economic Conditions in Japan—Harold Thompson interview
subfiles.from: Harold B. Schlammer, Twelfth Naval District
subfiles.about: Records Harold Thompson’s assessment of Japanese oil reserves, German influence, food supply, morale, and foreign policy.
subfiles.summary: Thompson claims Japan has roughly a year’s wartime oil reserve and describes Germans acquiring influential positions in business, censorship, policing, education, the army, and the navy. He reports that food and clothing remained obtainable in many areas despite poor government management, while rural hardship and dissatisfaction with the China war had damaged morale. He expects the pro-German Matsuoka to be replaced by the more pro-American and pro-British Mamoru Shigemitsu and argues that Japan does not want war with the United States.

subfiles.title: Navy memorandum transmitting an additional report on Japanese economic conditions
subfiles.from: H. F. Kingman, Office of Naval Intelligence
subfiles.about: Forwards another report on Japanese economic conditions for State Department use.
subfiles.summary: The short memorandum identifies the attached material as potentially useful to Orme Wilson. A notation indicates that a copy was also sent to the Treasury Department.

subfiles.title: Statement of Julio Jesus Passas Coelho on economic conditions in Japan
subfiles.from: Julio Jesus Passas Coelho
subfiles.about: Describes Japanese rationing, material shortages, business hardship, police corruption, and political disillusionment.
subfiles.summary: Coelho reports confused food rationing, shortages of potatoes, textiles, leather, gasoline, tin, and nonferrous metals, and widespread use of charcoal fuel and substitute materials. He says police corruption and pervasive regulations burden merchants, while the departure of British and American residents reduced foreign-exchange earnings and employment. According to business gossip, public frustration with the China war and the German-Japanese pact might bring the resignation of Konoe and Matsuoka and a government friendlier to the United States.

subfiles.title: Liaison Office note on the Navy reproduction restriction
subfiles.from: Under Secretary’s Liaison Office
subfiles.about: Clarifies that a Navy restriction on reproducing intelligence material does not apply to the State Department, FBI, or Military Intelligence Division.
subfiles.summary: The writer reports discussing the reproduction-control stamp with Captain Kingman. Kingman advised that the restriction was not intended to prevent use by the State Department, FBI, or MID.

subfiles.title: Illegible handwritten routing fragment
subfiles.about: A largely illegible routing or annotation sheet associated with the surrounding economic-intelligence material.
subfiles.summary: Only the Division of Far Eastern Affairs stamp and a few fragmentary handwritten words are legible. The page contains no recoverable substantive report.

subfiles.title: FBI letter transmitting a report from a source close to Saburō Kurusu
subfiles.from: J. Edgar Hoover, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Forwards an FBI memorandum based on a source closely connected with Japanese special envoy Saburō Kurusu.
subfiles.summary: The letter presents the enclosed information as potentially useful to Assistant Secretary Berle. It identifies the source only by the source’s close connection with Kurusu.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Japan’s weakened financial structure
subfiles.from: Federal Bureau of Investigation confidential source
subfiles.about: Reports claims that Japan’s finances were dangerously weak and that Kurusu’s mission sought to avert a worsening crisis.
subfiles.summary: A source close to Kurusu states that Japan could not seek help from American financial interests because doing so would reveal weakness and harden the U.S. negotiating position. The source reportedly admits that Kurusu came to the United States to address an extremely serious situation but nevertheless predicts that there will be no war.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note: Japan’s war potential
subfiles.from: Department of State records
subfiles.about: Cross-references a London telegram requesting American cooperation with a British study of Japan’s ability to wage war under blockade.
subfiles.summary: The note states that the Ministry of Economic Warfare had begun a special study of Japanese war potential within a wider examination of Japan’s industrial economy. It points researchers to telegram no. 5727 in file 894.20/272.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 5727: British questions concerning Japan’s war potential
subfiles.from: John G. Winant, London
subfiles.about: Requests U.S. information needed for a British study of Japan’s capacity to maintain military operations under blockade.
subfiles.summary: The Ministry of Economic Warfare seeks detailed data on iron and steel, ore deposits, coke, synthetic oil, mining labor, civilian morale, transportation, Southeast Asian minerals, material stocks, explosives, and automobile production. Its questions cover Japan, Korea, Manchukuo, China, Indochina, and Thailand and focus on current output, planned capacity, bottlenecks, and German technical support. The matter was also discussed with the U.S. military attaché for referral to War Department G-2.

subfiles.title: FBI letter transmitting miscellaneous Japanese information
subfiles.from: J. Edgar Hoover, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Forwards a confidential-source memorandum concerning industrial, transport, labor, and shipping conditions involving Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hoover sends the memorandum to Berle as potentially useful Japanese information. Copies were also directed to T. S. Wilkinson at the Office of Naval Intelligence and Sherman Miles at War Department G-2.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of miscellaneous information concerning Japan
subfiles.from: Federal Bureau of Investigation confidential source
subfiles.about: Reports industrial cutbacks, reduced rail service, shipping shortages, Chinese labor movements, and severe delays at Tsuruga.
subfiles.summary: Fuel and electric-power shortages allegedly reduced Osaka spinning and Nagoya porcelain production to one-third of normal, halved train service, and closed a major Nagoya employer. The memorandum also reports plans by the Nanjing government to send Chinese workers to Germany, purchases of old ships in Hong Kong, and an estimated Japanese shortage of 1.5 million tons of shipping. Imported steel for the Japanese Army reportedly took two months to reach Tokyo from Tsuruga, where inadequate unloading facilities and poor handling caused serious delays and losses.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note: Economic conditions in France
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.about: Cross-references a memorandum reporting Mr. Grandgerard’s observations on economic conditions in France.
subfiles.summary: The source is identified as Mr. Grandgerard of the Otis Elevator Company in Japan. The original memorandum is filed under number 894.00/1146.

subfiles.title: Japan: Economic Estimate
subfiles.about: Begins a comprehensive assessment of Japan’s raw materials, foreign-trade dependence, productive capacity, agriculture, fishing, food supply, and livestock.
subfiles.summary: The estimate opens with a commodity balance, table of contents, and index, then argues that scarce raw materials and dependence on silk exports, imported cotton, and foreign markets make Japan vulnerable to trade disruption. It treats Manchukuo and occupied parts of China as components of Japan’s wartime economic system but concludes that even this enlarged sphere could not achieve full economic independence. The surviving pages analyze limited arable land, rice imports, fishing and canned-fish exports, fuel and equipment shortages in the fishing industry, recent food shortages, and livestock production before continuing beyond this section.
